_note: main idea — 짧은 학술 토크. 1인 발화 45~55초.
각 지문은 사실 나열이 아니라 '마지막에 도달하는 하나의 통찰'을 갖도록 썼다.
오답은 전부 지문에 나온 수치·사례·비교이며, 그것들은 통찰을 받치는 근거일 뿐이다.
듣기는 되돌아갈 수 없으므로 주제문을 첫 문장에 두지 않는다.

turns.t: A honeybee comes back to the hive and starts walking in a figure eight. For a long time people thought this was just excitement. It isn't. The straight run through the middle of the eight points toward the food, but not toward where the bee is standing - toward the angle between the food and the sun. And the length of that straight run tells the others how far. A short run means close by. A long run means a long flight. So in a few seconds, in the dark, on a vertical wall, one bee gives another two separate numbers. It's not a celebration. It's a set of directions.

items.stem: What is the talk mainly about?
choices: How the bee dance communicates direction and distance
Why bees become excited after finding food
How dark the inside of a beehive is
How far bees can fly in a single trip
items.explanation: '흥분한 몸짓'이라는 통념은 두 번째 문장에서 부정된다. 요지는 춤이 방향과 거리라는 두 정보를 동시에 전달한다는 것.

turns.t: Cut a tree across and you see rings. Everyone knows you can count them for the age. That's the least interesting thing they tell you. A wide ring means a good year - warm, wet, plenty of growing. A narrow one means a hard year. And because trees in the same region go through the same weather, their patterns match. Match enough overlapping trees, living ones and old beams from buildings, and you can push a weather record back thousands of years, one year at a time. The tree wasn't trying to keep a diary. It just grew, and the growing recorded the weather.

items.stem: What is the speaker's main point?
choices: Tree rings can be used to find a tree's age
Wide rings mean warm and wet years
Old buildings contain useful wooden beams
Tree rings preserve a long record of past climate
items.explanation: 나이 세기는 '가장 재미없는 것'이라고 직접 낮춘다. 요지는 나이테가 수천 년치 기후 기록이 된다는 것.

turns.t: How does a bird cross an ocean and arrive at the same field it left last year? For decades researchers looked for the answer - singular. Is it the stars? Is it magnetism? Is it smell? The experiments kept giving messy results. Block the stars and the bird still gets there. Disturb the magnetic sense and it still gets there, just less precisely. It turned out the question was wrong. A migrating bird uses several systems at once and leans on whichever is working. Cloudy night, use magnetism. Magnetic noise, use the coastline. No single system is the answer, and that redundancy is exactly why it works.

items.stem: What is the main idea of the talk?
choices: Birds navigate mainly by the stars
Magnetism is the most reliable guide for birds
Birds rely on several overlapping systems rather than one
Cloudy nights make migration impossible
items.explanation: 각 실험이 '하나의 답'을 찾는 데 실패한 이유가 요지로 이어진다 — 여러 체계를 겹쳐 쓰기 때문에 하나를 막아도 도달한다.

turns.t: Look at a desert plant and you'll notice the leaves are tiny, or thin like needles, or missing entirely. That seems backwards. Leaves are where a plant makes food, so wouldn't you want more of them? Here's the catch. Leaves are also where water escapes. A big flat leaf in the desert loses water faster than the roots can replace it. So desert plants trade away food-making for water-keeping. The cactus went furthest: no leaves at all, and the green stem does the work instead. Every spine you see is a leaf that gave up its job entirely.

items.stem: What is the talk mainly explaining?
choices: Why desert plants have small or no leaves
How cactus spines protect against animals
Where plants make their food
How deep desert plant roots grow
items.explanation: 가시의 방어 기능이나 뿌리 이야기는 나오지 않는다. 요지는 '물을 지키려고 잎을 포기한 거래'다.

turns.t: A coral reef looks like rock, but it's built by animals - tiny ones, each in its own cup of limestone. What's strange is where a coral gets its energy. It catches some food with its tentacles, but most of what it needs comes from algae living inside its own tissue. The algae make sugar from sunlight and hand it over; the coral gives them shelter and raw materials. Neither does well alone. And this is why warming water is so dangerous. When the water gets too hot, the coral expels the algae, turns white, and starves - not from lack of food in the sea, but from losing its partner.

items.stem: What is the main point of the talk?
choices: Coral depends on a partnership that heat can break
Coral reefs are made of limestone
Coral catches food with its tentacles
Warming oceans are rising in temperature worldwide
items.explanation: 석회질·촉수는 배경 설명이다. 요지는 공생 관계가 산호의 생존 조건이며 수온 상승이 그 관계를 끊는다는 것.

turns.t: A bat flying through a dark cave sends out a click and listens for the echo. Simple enough. But think about what that means for speed. Sound takes time to travel out and come back, so the bat is always hearing where things were a moment ago, not where they are. To catch a moth that changes direction, the bat has to click faster and faster as it closes in - dozens of times a second at the end. It's not seeing with sound so much as constantly correcting a slightly outdated picture. Every hunt is a race between the echo and the moth.

items.stem: What is the speaker mainly explaining?
choices: That echolocation always lags slightly behind reality
That bats are blind in the dark
How loud a bat's clicks are
Why moths change direction when hunted
items.explanation: 요지는 '메아리는 항상 조금 과거의 정보'라서 박쥐가 끊임없이 보정해야 한다는 것이다. 박쥐가 눈이 멀었다는 말은 나오지 않는다.

turns.t: Ask anyone what's in a camel's hump and most will say water. It's fat. And that turns out to be more useful than water would be. Fat is dense energy, so the camel can go a long time without eating. But here's the clever part: storing it all in one place on the back, instead of spreading it under the skin like most mammals, means the rest of the body isn't wrapped in an insulating layer. Heat escapes. In a desert, being able to dump heat matters as much as having fuel. The hump solves two problems with one arrangement.

items.stem: What is the main idea?
choices: The hump's location solves both energy and heat problems
Camels store water in their humps
Camels can survive a long time without eating
Most mammals store fat under their skin
items.explanation: '물이 아니라 지방'에서 끝나지 않는다. 요지는 '한 군데에 몰아 둔 위치' 덕분에 열까지 버릴 수 있다는 두 가지 이점이다.

turns.t: Emperor penguins survive the Antarctic winter by huddling. Thousands of birds press together, and the temperature inside the huddle can reach twenty degrees while it's minus forty outside. The obvious question is who gets stuck on the edge. If the same birds were always outside, they'd die. So the huddle moves. Slowly, constantly, birds on the windward edge shuffle along the side and tuck into the back, and the whole mass drifts across the ice. Nobody is directing it. Each bird just steps toward warmth, and out of thousands of selfish little steps, everyone takes a turn in the cold.

items.stem: What is the talk mainly about?
choices: How a huddle shares the cold edge without any leader
How cold Antarctic winters become
Why emperor penguins live in Antarctica
How penguins find their way across the ice
items.explanation: 영하 40도라는 수치는 조건 설명이다. 요지는 지휘자 없이 개별 행동만으로 바깥 자리가 공평하게 돌아간다는 것.

turns.t: Watch ants find food and within an hour they've usually got a straight line to it. No ant surveyed the ground. Here's how it happens. Ants wander randomly, and any ant that finds food lays a scent trail on the way home. Other ants follow scent, and they also add their own. Now, a shorter path gets walked more times in the same period, so it collects scent faster, so more ants choose it, so it collects even more. The long path fades. Nobody compared the routes. The shortest one simply won a race that it was always going to win.

items.stem: What is the speaker's main point?
choices: Ants can smell food from a long distance
Scent trails fade over time
Ants wander randomly before finding food
The shortest route emerges without any ant comparing routes
items.explanation: 무작위 탐색과 냄새 소멸은 과정의 일부다. 요지는 '아무도 비교하지 않았는데 최단 경로가 저절로 남는다'는 마지막 두 문장.

turns.t: In the 1970s, stretches of the Pacific coast turned into what researchers called urchin barrens - bare rock where kelp forests used to be. The urchins were eating the kelp. But urchins had always been there. What had changed was sea otters, hunted almost to nothing for their fur. Otters eat urchins. Remove the otter, the urchins multiply, the kelp disappears, and with it the fish that lived in it. Bring the otters back and the kelp returns within a decade. The lesson isn't about otters specifically. It's that removing one species can rearrange an entire coastline.

items.stem: What is the main idea of the talk?
choices: Sea otters were hunted for their fur
Removing one species can transform a whole ecosystem
Sea urchins eat kelp
Kelp forests recover within ten years
items.explanation: 마지막 두 문장이 요지를 직접 말한다 — '해달 이야기가 아니라, 한 종을 없애면 해안 전체가 바뀐다는 이야기'.

turns.t: People say no two snowflakes are alike, and it sounds like a nice thing people just say. There's a reason behind it. A snowflake starts as a speck of dust and grows as it falls, and the shape it takes at each moment depends on the exact temperature and humidity right there. Fall a few centimeters and those conditions change slightly, and the crystal responds. So the finished flake is a record of the particular path it fell through. Two flakes would have to take identical journeys through a constantly shifting sky. That's the real claim - not magic, just a very long list of conditions.

items.stem: What is the speaker mainly explaining?
choices: Why snowflakes are six-sided
How dust particles enter the atmosphere
Why each snowflake records its own falling path
How fast snowflakes fall to the ground
items.explanation: 요지는 눈송이 모양이 낙하 경로의 조건을 기록한 결과라는 것이다. 육각형 구조나 낙하 속도는 언급되지 않는다.

turns.t: Earthworms don't look like they're doing much. Charles Darwin spent almost forty years studying them, which tells you he disagreed. A worm pulls dead leaves down into the soil, digests them, and leaves the remains behind as it tunnels. Those tunnels let air and water reach roots. Darwin measured how much soil worms move and calculated that on ordinary farmland they turn over the top layer completely every few decades. He called them nature's plough. The point is that the most important work in a field can be done by something you'd step over without noticing.

items.stem: What is the main idea?
choices: Darwin studied earthworms for forty years
Earthworms quietly do essential work in the soil
Worm tunnels let water reach plant roots
Farmland needs to be ploughed every few decades
items.explanation: 다윈의 40년과 터널 이야기는 근거다. 마지막 문장이 요지를 직접 말한다 — 눈에 띄지 않는 것이 가장 중요한 일을 한다.

turns.t: A seed that sprouts as soon as it hits the ground sounds efficient. In many places it's a fatal mistake. Imagine a seed dropping in autumn during a warm spell. Sprout now and the first frost kills you. So many seeds have a lock: they will not germinate until they've experienced a long cold period, or been soaked repeatedly, or even passed through a fire. Those conditions are a rough signal that the dangerous season has actually ended. The seed isn't sleeping because it's slow. Waiting is the strategy, and the lock is what makes the waiting reliable.

items.stem: What is the talk mainly about?
choices: How frost damages young plants
Why some seeds delay sprouting until conditions are right
Which seeds need fire to germinate
How long seeds can survive in soil
items.explanation: 서리·불은 예시다. 요지는 마지막 두 문장 — 휴면은 게으름이 아니라 전략이며 조건 잠금이 그 전략을 신뢰할 수 있게 만든다.

turns.t: An octopus changes color in a fraction of a second to match a rock, a patch of sand, a piece of coral. Here's the part that keeps biologists up at night. As far as we can tell, octopuses are colorblind - their eyes have only one type of light receptor. So how does an animal that cannot see color match color? One idea is that the skin itself detects light; the same light-sensitive proteins found in eyes turn up in octopus skin. If that's right, the octopus isn't looking at its surroundings and copying them. It's feeling the light on its body and responding, without the picture ever reaching its brain.

items.stem: What is the central puzzle in the talk?
choices: How octopuses change color so quickly
Why octopuses hide among rocks and coral
Where light-sensitive proteins are usually found
How a colorblind animal can match colors
items.explanation: 속도는 도입부의 사실이고, 강연의 중심 질문은 '색을 못 보는 동물이 어떻게 색을 맞추는가'이다.

turns.t: Monarch butterflies travel from Canada to central Mexico, thousands of kilometers, and arrive at a handful of specific forest groves. Now here's what makes it strange. The butterfly that arrives is not the one that left. It's usually the great-grandchild. The northward trip in spring takes three or four short-lived generations, each going part of the way and laying eggs. Then one long-lived generation makes the entire return flight south. So no individual butterfly has ever seen the destination, and none can have learned the route from a parent it never met. Whatever the map is, it isn't memory.

items.stem: What is the speaker mainly pointing out?
choices: Monarchs travel thousands of kilometers each year
Monarchs spend the winter in Mexican forests
Some monarch generations live longer than others
The route cannot be learned, since no butterfly makes the full trip
items.explanation: 세대 교체와 수명 차이는 근거다. 요지는 마지막 문장 — 목적지를 본 개체가 없으므로 그 지도는 기억일 수 없다.

turns.t: We always see the same face of the moon. Not because the moon doesn't rotate - it does. It rotates exactly once for every orbit around Earth, so the same side stays pointed at us. That's not a coincidence. Earth's gravity pulls harder on the near side of the moon than the far side, which slightly stretches it, and over a very long time that stretching acted like a brake on the moon's spin. It slowed until the rotation matched the orbit, and then there was nothing left to slow. Most large moons in the solar system have ended up locked the same way.

items.stem: What is the talk mainly explaining?
choices: That the moon does not rotate at all
Why the same side of the moon always faces us
How long the moon takes to orbit Earth
How many moons exist in the solar system
items.explanation: '달이 자전하지 않는다'는 통념은 두 번째 문장에서 부정된다. 요지는 조석력이 자전을 늦춰 공전과 같아졌다는 설명이다.

turns.t: People live on the slopes of active volcanoes, which sounds like a failure of judgment until you look at the soil. Volcanic ash is packed with minerals that plants need, and unlike ordinary rock, it breaks down fast. Within a few decades of an eruption, land that was buried can grow better crops than it did before. So farmers came back, generation after generation, because the same mountain that destroyed the village also made the fields rich. It isn't that people forgot the danger. They weighed a rare disaster against reliable harvests, and the harvests won.

items.stem: What is the main point?
choices: Volcanic eruptions destroy farming villages
Volcanic ash contains minerals plants need
People settle near volcanoes because the soil is unusually fertile
Eruptions happen only rarely in most regions
items.explanation: 무기질 함량은 근거이고, 요지는 사람들이 위험을 잊은 게 아니라 저울질한 끝에 화산 곁에 산다는 것이다.

turns.t: Rivers on flat land almost never run straight, and it isn't because something is in the way. Start with a perfectly straight channel and the tiniest bend will appear anyway. Water moving around the outside of a bend travels faster and cuts into that bank; water on the inside slows and drops sand. So the bend deepens itself. Every curve makes the next curve more likely. Eventually the loops get so extreme that the river cuts across the neck and abandons the loop, leaving a crescent lake behind. The river isn't avoiding obstacles. It's producing its own shape.

items.stem: What is the talk mainly about?
choices: How crescent-shaped lakes are used
Which rivers are the longest on flat land
How fast water moves around a bend
Why rivers curve even without obstacles
items.explanation: 장애물 때문이 아니라는 점을 두 번 짚는다. 요지는 강이 스스로 굽이를 만들어 낸다는 것.

turns.t: When you look at a star you are not looking at a star. You're looking at light that left it. For the nearest ones that's a few years; for others, thousands. Some of the light arriving tonight started out before there were cities anywhere on Earth. This means a few odd things are true at once. A star you can see might not exist anymore. And nothing you can point at in the night sky is happening now - the whole view is a collage of different pasts, arranged by distance. Astronomers don't find this troubling. It's the only way to look backward in time.

items.stem: What is the speaker's main point?
choices: Some stars are only a few light years away
Astronomers study stars that no longer exist
City lights make stars harder to see
The night sky shows many different moments in the past
items.explanation: 요지는 밤하늘 전체가 거리에 따라 배열된 '서로 다른 과거들의 모음'이라는 것이다. 사라진 별은 그 결과 중 하나다.

turns.t: Nobody has ever been more than about twelve kilometers into the Earth. So how do we claim to know there's a liquid layer thousands of kilometers down? Earthquakes. A quake sends two kinds of waves through the planet, and one of them cannot travel through liquid. When a large quake happens, stations on the far side of the globe record an area where that wave simply never arrives - a shadow. The size and shape of that shadow tells you where the liquid begins and ends. We didn't drill down to the core. We read its outline in the waves that failed to show up.

items.stem: What is the main idea?
choices: Earthquakes cause serious damage worldwide
Drilling has reached twelve kilometers deep
The Earth's interior is known from waves that fail to arrive
Two kinds of waves travel at different speeds
items.explanation: 굴착 깊이와 파동 종류는 근거다. 요지는 마지막 문장 — 도달하지 못한 파동의 그림자로 내부 구조를 읽어 냈다는 것.

turns.t: The Silk Road is usually pictured as camels carrying silk west and gold east. That happened. But the goods were the least durable part of the exchange. Along those same routes traveled papermaking, which reached the Mediterranean from China; the number system we now call Arabic, which came from India; techniques for casting metal; and, less happily, diseases. A merchant carried a bolt of cloth once and it was worn out in a decade. He carried a method for making paper once and it was still in use a thousand years later. The road's real cargo was knowledge, and nobody was charging for it.

items.stem: What is the speaker mainly arguing?
choices: Silk was the most valuable trade good of the period
Diseases spread quickly along trade routes
Ideas traveling the route mattered more than the goods
Paper was invented in the Mediterranean
items.explanation: 비단 교역은 인정하되 '가장 오래가지 못한 부분'이라고 낮춘다. 요지는 진짜 화물은 지식이었다는 마지막 문장이다.

turns.t: Before printing, English spelling was a free-for-all. The same writer might spell one word three ways on a single page, and nobody thought that was wrong - you spelled it the way it sounded to you. Then printing arrived, and a printer setting type had to choose one version. Choosing took time, so printers settled on habits, and those habits spread with the books. Within a couple of generations, spellings that had been personal became fixed - including some odd ones that got frozen in place by accident. The rules you're marked wrong on today were mostly a printer's convenience, not a decision about correctness.

items.stem: What is the main point of the talk?
choices: Printing made books cheaper to produce
English spelling became fixed through printers' habits
Writers used to spell words however they liked
Some English words are spelled illogically
items.explanation: 자유로운 철자와 이상한 철자는 앞뒤 사실이고, 요지는 인쇄공의 편의가 철자를 고정시켰다는 인과다.

turns.t: A Roman aqueduct could carry water fifty kilometers into a city, and it did it without a single pump. The trick is a slope so gentle you could not see it - in some sections the drop is about thirty centimeters per kilometer. Any steeper and the water would rush, wearing away the channel; any flatter and it would sit still. Surveyors had to hold that fraction of a degree across mountains and valleys, using water levels and sighting tools. The impressive part isn't the tall stone arches everyone photographs. It's the invisible precision of the slope those arches were built to protect.

items.stem: What does the speaker emphasize most?
choices: The height of the stone arches
How far water traveled into Roman cities
The precise gentle slope that made the system work
That Romans had no pumps available
items.explanation: 아치는 '사진 찍는 부분'으로 낮추고, 요지는 눈에 보이지 않는 경사의 정밀함이라고 마지막 문장에서 못 박는다.

turns.t: Mail used to be sorted entirely by reading addresses, which meant a clerk had to know where every town and street was. As cities grew, that became impossible. The answer was to give places numbers. A postal code turns a sentence a human has to interpret into a short code a machine can sort. And once machines could sort, mail volume could grow without hiring more clerks who knew the map by heart. It's a small invention with an odd shape: it didn't make delivery faster by moving letters faster. It made it faster by changing what the letter had to say.

items.stem: What is the main idea?
choices: Cities grew too large in the last century
Mail clerks memorized street names
Postal codes let machines sort mail instead of people
Letters travel faster than they used to
items.explanation: 마지막 두 문장이 요지를 정리한다 — 편지를 빨리 옮긴 게 아니라 편지에 적히는 정보를 바꿔 기계 분류를 가능하게 했다.

turns.t: For most of history every town kept its own time, set by the sun overhead. Noon in one city was a few minutes off from noon in the next, and nobody minded, because nobody could travel fast enough for it to matter. Railways changed that overnight. A train leaving at ten and arriving at two crossed a dozen local noons, and timetables became unusable - there were real collisions caused by clocks that disagreed. So the railway companies, not governments, drew up standard time zones and simply started using them. Cities adopted the railway's time because the trains would not wait.

items.stem: What is the speaker mainly explaining?
choices: How railways forced the adoption of standard time
Why local time varied from town to town
That train timetables are difficult to read
That governments created the first time zones
items.explanation: 정부가 아니라 철도회사가 먼저 만들었다고 직접 말한다. 요지는 철도가 표준시를 강제했다는 인과다.

turns.t: An early lighthouse burned wood or coal, and the light was pitiful - visible a few kilometers on a clear night, useless in the weather that actually sinks ships. Making the fire bigger barely helped, because light spreads in every direction and most of it goes up into the sky or down into the rock. The breakthrough wasn't a brighter flame. It was a lens made of stepped rings that caught light heading the wrong way and bent it into a flat horizontal beam. Same fire, twenty times the reach. The problem had never been how much light there was. It was where the light was going.

items.stem: What is the main point?
choices: Early lighthouses burned wood and coal
Directing the light mattered more than increasing it
Storms are the most dangerous time for ships
Lenses are made of stepped glass rings
items.explanation: 마지막 두 문장이 요지다 — 빛의 양이 아니라 빛의 방향이 문제였다.

turns.t: Paper was invented in China from mulberry bark and rags, and for centuries it stayed there. When it reached the Islamic world and then Europe, something interesting happened: it had to be reinvented, because the local materials were different. European papermakers used old linen clothing, and the supply of paper depended on the supply of worn-out shirts. Cities passed laws about collecting rags. So the spread of writing in Europe was tied, for a while, to how much cloth people threw away. A technology doesn't simply move from place to place. It gets rebuilt out of whatever the new place has.

items.stem: What is the main idea of the talk?
choices: Paper was first made in China
European cities passed laws about collecting rags
Linen makes better paper than mulberry bark
A technology is rebuilt from local materials as it spreads
items.explanation: 중국 기원과 넝마 수집법은 근거다. 마지막 두 문장이 요지를 직접 말한다 — 기술은 옮겨지는 게 아니라 그 지역 재료로 다시 만들어진다.

turns.t: In the 1600s a new drink arrived in London and with it a new kind of room. Coffeehouses charged a penny at the door, and inside, anyone could sit at any table. That was the unusual part. A merchant, a doctor, and a sailor might share a bench, and the rule was that you spoke to whoever was there. News circulated, arguments happened, and several of the first newspapers began as sheets written up from coffeehouse talk. Some were called penny universities, and not entirely as a joke. What was being sold was the coffee. What people came for was the conversation.

items.stem: What is the speaker mainly describing?
choices: How coffee was first brought to London
Why newspapers were expensive at first
How coffeehouses became places where information spread
How much a cup of coffee cost in the 1600s
items.explanation: 커피 도입과 1페니는 배경이다. 요지는 마지막 두 문장 — 팔린 것은 커피였지만 사람들이 온 이유는 대화였다.

turns.t: Long before anyone understood germs, farmers in England noticed something odd: milkmaids rarely caught smallpox. They did catch cowpox, a mild disease from cattle, and it left them marked but healthy. A country doctor took that piece of local gossip seriously enough to test it, deliberately exposing a boy to cowpox and then to smallpox. The boy did not fall ill. Nobody at the time could explain why it worked - the immune system wouldn't be understood for another century. The method arrived long before the theory, which is more common in medicine than we like to admit.

items.stem: What is the main point?
choices: Cowpox is a mild disease caught from cattle
Milkmaids were healthier than other workers
A working method can come before the explanation for it
Smallpox was the deadliest disease in England
items.explanation: 우두와 젖 짜는 여성 이야기는 사례다. 요지는 마지막 문장 — 의학에서는 이론보다 방법이 먼저 도착하는 일이 드물지 않다.

turns.t: Look at a European painting from the year 1300 and something feels off. Important people are enormous, distant buildings float, and the floor tilts up at you. The painters weren't bad at seeing. They were showing importance, not space - the king is big because he's the king. Then artists worked out a system of lines converging on a single point, and suddenly a flat wall could hold a room you seem able to walk into. But notice the cost. Once size means distance, it can't also mean importance. Gaining depth meant giving up a language painters had used for a thousand years.

items.stem: What is the speaker mainly explaining?
choices: Medieval painters lacked the skill to draw properly
Perspective gained realism but gave up an older visual language
Kings were often the subject of medieval paintings
Lines converging on a point create the illusion of depth
items.explanation: '못 그린 게 아니다'라고 직접 부정한다. 요지는 원근법이 깊이를 얻는 대신 크기로 중요도를 나타내던 언어를 잃었다는 교환이다.

turns.t: For most of human history music existed only while someone was performing it. A song survived if people remembered it, and it changed a little every time it was passed on. Written notation changed the relationship. Once a melody could be fixed on a page, a composer could write something too long and too complicated for anyone to hold in memory, and it would still be performed correctly a century later in a city he'd never visited. But something was lost too: the small variations each singer added stopped being part of the piece and started being mistakes.

items.stem: What is the main idea?
choices: Composers wrote longer pieces than singers could remember
Music used to be passed down by memory
Notation let music become larger and fixed, but less flexible
Singers often made mistakes before notation existed
items.explanation: 기억 전승과 긴 곡은 앞뒤 사실이다. 요지는 마지막 문장까지 포함한 '고정성을 얻고 변주를 잃었다'는 양면이다.

turns.t: Ask speakers of different languages to sort colored chips and you don't get the same piles. Some languages have one word covering both blue and green. Russian has two separate basic words where English has one blue. And this isn't just labeling - speakers of a language with two blues are measurably faster at telling those two shades apart. But be careful with that finding. Everyone sees the same wavelengths; nobody is colorblind because of grammar. What differs is which boundaries you've practiced noticing. Language doesn't change the eye. It changes what the eye has had reason to pay attention to.

items.stem: What is the speaker mainly arguing?
choices: Language shapes attention to color, not the eye itself
Some languages have no word for blue
Russian speakers see more colors than English speakers
Color words are the same across most languages
items.explanation: '문법 때문에 색맹이 되지는 않는다'고 직접 경계한다. 요지는 마지막 두 문장 — 언어가 바꾸는 것은 눈이 아니라 주의를 기울여 온 경계다.

turns.t: Roman numerals have no zero, and for counting sheep you don't need one. The trouble starts when you want to write numbers by position. In our system, the 3 in 305 means three hundreds because of where it sits, and the 0 is what holds that place open. Without a symbol for nothing, you cannot tell 35 from 305. So zero isn't really a number in that role - it's a piece of punctuation that makes position meaningful. Cultures that developed place-value systems had to invent it, and the ones that didn't stayed stuck doing arithmetic that we'd find nearly impossible.

items.stem: What is the main point about zero?
choices: Zero makes a place-value number system possible
Zero was unknown to the Romans
Roman numerals cannot express large numbers
Zero means the same as nothing
items.explanation: 로마 숫자는 대조 사례다. 요지는 0이 '자리를 열어 두는 표시'로서 자릿값 체계를 성립시킨다는 것.

turns.t: Every flat map of the world is wrong, and it has to be. You cannot flatten the surface of a sphere without stretching or tearing it somewhere - that's a mathematical fact, not a failure of cartography. So every projection chooses what to sacrifice. The familiar classroom map keeps directions correct, which is what a sailor needs, and pays for it by inflating everything near the poles until Greenland looks the size of Africa. Another projection keeps areas honest and bends the shapes instead. The right question about a map is never whether it's accurate. It's which distortion it chose, and for whom.

items.stem: What is the speaker's main point?
choices: Every map projection must choose which distortion to accept
Greenland is much smaller than it appears
Classroom maps should be replaced
Sailors need maps with correct directions
items.explanation: 그린란드와 항해용 지도는 예시다. 요지는 마지막 두 문장 — 정확한가가 아니라 어떤 왜곡을 누구를 위해 골랐는가를 물어야 한다.

turns.t: When photography arrived in the 1800s, portrait painters had a problem. A photograph produced a likeness in minutes, cheaper and more accurate than weeks of sitting still. A lot of painters left the profession. But look at what painting did next. Within a few decades you get work that is deliberately blurred, or flattened, or wildly colored - things a camera could not do and would not want to do. Losing the job of copying appearances freed painting to ask what else a picture could be. The competition didn't kill it. It pushed it toward the part that was never mechanical.

items.stem: What is the main idea?
choices: Photography made portrait painters lose their jobs
Early photographs were cheaper than paintings
Painters in the 1800s used brighter colors
Photography pushed painting toward what a camera cannot do
items.explanation: 화가들이 직업을 잃은 것은 사실이지만 마지막 세 문장이 요지를 뒤집는다 — 경쟁이 회화를 기계가 못 하는 영역으로 밀어붙였다.

turns.t: Bamboo isn't a tree. It's a grass, and that single fact explains most of what's surprising about it. A tree adds a thin ring of wood each year, which is why it takes decades to get tall. A grass grows from segments that all lengthen at once, so some bamboo species add most of their final height in a single season - you can measure the change between morning and evening. It also means bamboo doesn't thicken as it ages; a shoot comes out of the ground at its final width. Everything odd about bamboo follows from what kind of plant it is.

items.stem: What is the talk mainly about?
choices: How tall bamboo can grow in one season
How being a grass explains bamboo's unusual growth
Why trees take decades to grow tall
How bamboo is used for building
items.explanation: 성장 속도와 나무 비교는 근거다. 첫 문장과 마지막 문장이 함께 요지를 감싼다 — 벼과 식물이라는 사실이 특이한 성질을 설명한다.

turns.t: A desert beetle in Namibia drinks fog. It climbs a dune at night, tilts its body forward, and holds still while fog rolls in. Its back is covered in tiny bumps that water clings to, and between them are waxy channels that water slides down straight to its mouth. No pump, no energy spent - just a surface shaped so that water has nowhere else to go. Engineers have copied that pattern onto mesh panels to pull drinking water out of coastal fog. The beetle didn't have a better idea than us. It had a better surface, and the idea was sitting on it the whole time.

items.stem: What is the main point of the talk?
choices: Fog is common along the Namibian coast
A surface shape alone can collect water, and engineers copied it
The beetle spends a lot of energy collecting water
Desert beetles drink at night to avoid heat
items.explanation: 에너지를 쓰지 않는다고 직접 말하므로 소모 관련 선택지는 오답이다. 요지는 '표면 구조만으로 물을 모으며 그 원리가 공학에 옮겨졌다'는 것.
